title: The Colonial Pressure Cooker
bullets: Spanish America in 1800 was not seething to leave the empire; most of its future revolutionaries wanted a better deal inside the system, not a way out, and the empire fell only when its head was cut off in Europe.

Starting with Columbus in 1492 and the conquests of the Aztec and Inca, Spain assembled the largest empire yet seen, running two continents from the future U.S. southwest to Patagonia, all held together by loyalty to one distant king.

Spain ruled through viceroyalties — giant provinces run by a viceroy, a stand-in for the king — and the four big ones (New Spain, Peru, New Granada, and the Río de la Plata, created in 1776) became the rough ancestors of the future nations.

The casta system sorted everyone by ancestry into a fixed racial ladder, with peninsulares (Spanish-born) at the top, creoles (American-born Spaniards) just below, then mestizos, mulattoes, Indigenous peoples, and enslaved Africans at the bottom.

The grievance that mattered most was between peninsulares and creoles: the American-born elite owned the estates and mines but watched the best offices handed to freshly arrived Spaniards, and resented being second-class subjects in their own land.

The empire's economic engine was silver, above all the mountain at Potosí, dug out under the brutal mita labor draft the Spanish had twisted from the Inca — proof that the colonies existed, by design, to be drained.

The well-meaning Bourbon Reforms of the later 1700s backfired: by raising taxes, tightening monopolies, and staffing new offices with peninsulares, they convinced the creole elite that the crown saw them as a cow to be milked.

Three early sparks lit and were stamped out — Túpac Amaru II's massive Andean uprising of 1780, the genteel Inconfidência Mineira plot of 1789 (which made a martyr of Tiradentes), and Bahia's bottom-up Tailors' Revolt of 1798.

Enlightenment ideas about rights and the consent of the governed seeped in through smuggled books, the data of the traveling naturalist Alexander von Humboldt, and Antonio Nariño's contraband translation of the Rights of Man.

By 1807 everything for an explosion was present except a trigger, and nobody inside the empire was reaching for one — what broke it would come from outside: a slave revolt in the Caribbean and a French army marching into Spain.

title: Haiti Lights the Fuse
bullets: The first nation in the Americas to break free of Europe was founded not by creole aristocrats quoting the Enlightenment but by enslaved people who picked up cane knives — and it terrified every other founder in this book.

Saint-Domingue, the French western third of Hispaniola, was the richest colony on earth in 1791, producing a third of the world's sugar by working its enslaved majority to death — a death machine, not the self-reproducing slavery of the mainland.

In August 1791 that enslaved majority rose, beginning the Haitian Revolution — the largest and only fully successful slave revolt in recorded history — burning the cane fields and turning the engine of French wealth into a war zone.

What made it the hinge event of the hemisphere is that it won against everyone: over thirteen years the formerly enslaved defeated the local French, a Spanish invasion, a British expedition, and finally Napoleon's own army.

The revolution found its great leader in Toussaint Louverture, enslaved into middle age, self-taught, a genius at war and politics, who played France, Spain, and Britain off one another before Napoleon lured him to a parley, seized him, and let him die in a freezing French prison in 1803.

Leadership passed to Louverture's hardened lieutenant Jean-Jacques Dessalines, and once it was clear the French had come to restore slavery the war turned total, with yellow fever scything through the European ranks and the Battle of Vertières shattering the last French force in late 1803.

On January 1, 1804, Dessalines proclaimed independence and named the nation Haiti, reaching back past the Europeans to the Taíno — a cascade of firsts, including the first nation ever founded by formerly enslaved people who freed themselves by arms.

The birth was not clean: Dessalines crowned himself emperor, ordered the 1804 massacre of most remaining white French, and was assassinated in 1806 — the revolution that ended one of history's worst crimes ended in a crime of its own.

Haiti became load-bearing for everything that followed — proof to the enslaved, nightmare to the slaveholders, the 'specter of Haiti' that made the creole revolutionaries so cautious about race because they had all seen what mass mobilization could do.

It was also the literal secret backer of the Spanish-American revolution: when Bolívar was a defeated exile with nothing, Haiti gave him ships, guns, a press, and men — on one condition, that he free the slaves wherever he won.

title: The Empire Decapitates Itself
bullets: The Spanish empire in 1808 was held together by a person, not an idea — every viceroy, judge, and officer held power only because the king in Madrid had granted it — and Napoleon reached out and removed that single point.
Trying to strangle Britain's trade, Napoleon sent his armies into the Iberian Peninsula, beginning the Peninsular War, and came first for Portugal in late 1807.

Rather than be captured, the entire Portuguese court — the prince regent (future John VI), the royal family, the government, the treasury, thousands of officials — fled across the Atlantic under British naval protection and re-established the monarchy in Rio de Janeiro.

For the first and only time in colonial history an empire was now ruled from its colony, which is why Brazil's road to independence would look nothing like Spanish America's: there was no decapitation, but a king who showed up in person.

In Spain, Napoleon lured the feuding royal family to Bayonne, bullied both Charles IV and his son Ferdinand VII into renouncing the throne, and installed his own brother Joseph Bonaparte as king — in weeks, the legitimate king became a prisoner.

The deposed Ferdinand VII became a symbol he had done nothing to earn — 'el Deseado,' the Desired One, the captive king around whom loyalty crystallized — though when he finally returned in 1814 he proved a vengeful absolutist who betrayed everyone who fought in his name.

Across unoccupied Spain, ordinary people refused to obey Joseph and formed local governing committees — juntas — reaching for the old idea that when the king cannot rule, sovereignty reverts to the people.

Holed up in Cádiz behind British ships, the Cortes set out to reinvent Spain as a liberal nation, inviting American delegates and producing the radical Constitution of 1812, which proclaimed sovereignty in the nation and taught the political vocabulary the revolutions would speak.

The same logic crossed the ocean as a loyalist argument — the colonists, too, would form juntas for the captive Ferdinand — but it contained a radioactive question: if sovereignty had reverted to Americans, why obey the juntas in Spain at all?

That is the decapitation: Spain lost its empire not because the colonies rose against a hated king but because the king was taken away, and the colonists improvising a government talked themselves, reluctantly then irreversibly, into ruling on their own.

title: The Juntas and the First Republics
bullets: 1810 was the year the dam broke nearly everywhere at once, as creole elites across Spanish America deposed their Spanish governors and set up juntas — but this is mostly a chapter of failure, of fragile first republics crushed within a year or two.

In Buenos Aires the May Revolution of 1810 deposed the viceroy and installed a creole junta that stuck, giving the southern revolution the one thing the north lacked — a secure home base the royalists never retook.

In Venezuela the revolution began with the most fervor: Caracas formed its junta in 1810, declared independence in 1811 as the first Spanish-American colony to do so, and made the old exile Francisco de Miranda leader of the First Venezuelan Republic.

That republic lasted barely a year, undone by too much federalism, a social order that gave the masses no reason to fight, and a catastrophic 1812 earthquake the Church called the wrath of God — and Miranda's own officers, Bolívar among them, handed the surrendering Precursor to the Spanish, who let him die in a dungeon.

Fleeing into exile, Bolívar wrote the Cartagena Manifesto, a clear-eyed autopsy blaming the republic's death on idealism — too much federalism, too little central authority — and forming the lifelong creed that liberty in Spanish America needed a firm, even authoritarian hand.

His 1813 Admirable Campaign retook Caracas, earned him the title El Libertador, and established a Second Venezuelan Republic — but to wage it he issued the chilling Decree of War to the Death, which licensed atrocity on both sides.

The Second Republic was destroyed not by Spain from across the sea but by Venezuelans: the royalist commander José Tomás Boves turned the mixed-race plains horsemen, the llaneros, into a ferocious cavalry that tore it apart in 1814 — proof the masses were not automatically anyone's allies.

The pattern repeated elsewhere — Belgrano won at Tucumán and Salta but failed to push into Upper Peru, teaching that royalist Peru could not be taken overland from the south, while the gaucho leader Artigas raised a federalist revolution in the Banda Oriental.

Then the king came back: with Napoleon beaten, the restored Ferdinand VII tore up the Constitution of 1812 and in 1815 sent the largest expedition Spain ever dispatched to the Americas — some 10,000 troops under Pablo Morillo — to reconquer the colonies.

Morillo's reconquest crushed the first republics but his terror — executions, confiscations, the shooting of moderates like Camilo Torres Tenorio — fell on exactly the hesitant creoles Spain needed, convincing many that the only safety lay in driving Spain out completely.

title: Bolívar's Northern Campaign
bullets: In 1815 Bolívar was, by any reasonable accounting, a failure — a defeated exile, broke and without an army, on the British island of Jamaica — yet within eleven years he would be master of an area larger than Napoleon's conquests and liberator of six future nations.

Born in 1783 into one of the richest creole families in Venezuela and raised by an Enlightenment tutor, Bolívar was short, intense, vain, tireless, and brilliant — a slaveholder by birth who became a genuine abolitionist by conviction and necessity.

In Jamaican exile he wrote the Jamaica Letter, the founding text of Latin American political thought, predicting independence with eerie accuracy and then warning that nations kept ignorant under colonial rule would fracture and fall to strongmen.

Prophecy does not free a continent, so Bolívar got guns and men from Haiti, whose president Alexandre Pétion gave him ships, weapons, a press, and volunteers — asking only that he proclaim abolition wherever his armies won.

He found his army where his enemy Boves had found one: the plains, allying with the illiterate, fearless llanero chieftain José Antonio Páez and adding the British Legion of unemployed Napoleonic veterans, so the plainsmen who had ridden for Spain now rode for the republic.

In 1819 he ran one of history's boldest gambles, marching across the flooded llanos and up over a frozen Andean pass above 13,000 feet — losing men and horses by the hundreds — to fall on the Spanish where they were certain no army could be.

Three days off the mountain, the Battle of Boyacá (August 7, 1819) was over in two hours: his army captured nearly the entire royalist force at a cost of fewer than a hundred casualties, breaking Spanish power in New Granada in a single afternoon.

At a congress in Angostura late in 1819 Bolívar realized his lifelong dream, proclaiming the union of Venezuela, New Granada, and Ecuador into the great state historians call Gran Colombia — magnificent on paper, but its distant regions barely knew one another.

Over the next three years his generals finished the north: Carabobo (1821) secured Venezuelan independence, Lake Maracaibo ended the seaborne threat in 1823, and his gifted lieutenant Sucre won Pichincha (1822) to liberate Ecuador.

Manuela Sáenz — a fierce, politically sharp woman whom the marble statues left out — became Bolívar's lover, confidante, and ally, a decorated revolutionary who would one night save his life and stand for the many women the histories of great men erased.

title: San Martín and the Southern Crossing
bullets: If Bolívar was the revolution's fire, José de San Martín was its ice — a man who built an army, crossed the Andes, won the decisive battles, then at the summit of triumph simply handed it all to his rival and walked away from public life forever.

Born in 1778 in the Río de la Plata and raised in Spain, San Martín spent over twenty years as a professional Spanish officer fighting the French before abandoning that career in 1812 to offer his sword to the revolution — arriving as a technician of war, not a firebrand.

His strategic insight was that Lima, the citadel of Spanish power, could not be taken overland from the south, as Belgrano's failures had proved; it had to be taken from the sea, which first meant liberating Chile and building a fleet.

As governor of the frontier province of Cuyo around Mendoza, he spent two patient years turning the whole province into a war machine, raising and drilling the Army of the Andes and recruiting Chilean exiles, chief among them Bernardo O'Higgins.

In January–February 1817 came the Crossing of the Andes, pushing 5,000 men over passes above 12,000 feet in coordinated columns with deliberate misinformation — an ordeal that killed a third of the animals but brought the army down where it was least expected.

Surprise was total: on February 12, 1817, San Martín smashed the royalists at Chacabuco and two days later entered Santiago, and O'Higgins became Supreme Director of a Chile that declared independence the following year.

The campaign nearly came undone at the night attack of Cancha Rayada in early 1818, but San Martín rallied the broken army and on April 5, 1818, annihilated the last royalist field force at Maipú, securing Chile's independence for good.

With Chile as a base, a navy under the flamboyant Scottish ex-officer Thomas Cochrane carried San Martín north; he entered Lima in July 1821, proclaimed Peru's independence, and took the deliberately modest title of 'Protector.'

But the Spanish armies had pulled back undefeated into the high Andes, and San Martín, lacking the strength to finish alone, needed Bolívar — so the two halves of the revolution finally converged at Guayaquil in July 1822.

At that famous closed-door meeting, of which no reliable record survives, San Martín yielded completely — giving up Guayaquil, his army, and the whole unfinished liberation of Peru to Bolívar — then withdrew into thirty years of obscure European exile, the liberator who refused to become a ruler.

title: The Final Reckoning
bullets: By late 1822 the Spanish empire in South America had shrunk to one stubborn fortress: the highlands of Peru, where the Spanish had pulled their main armies up into the high interior around Cusco, where thin air and brutal terrain made them hard to reach.

These were no demoralized garrisons but the largest, most experienced royalist field armies left on the continent, and so long as they survived intact the independence of all South America remained provisional.

Bolívar arrived in 1823 to a snake pit of quarreling Peruvian patriots, an empty treasury, and a royalist army even pushing back toward the coast — and spent much of 1823–24, granted near-dictatorial power, patiently rebuilding an army to fight in the high country.

The first clash, at Junín in August 1824, was one of the strangest battles of the era — fought above 13,000 feet almost entirely by cavalry, in near silence with lance and saber and not a shot fired — and it shattered royalist morale.

On December 9, 1824, the Battle of Ayacucho finished the war: Bolívar absent, his finest general Antonio José de Sucre broke a larger royalist line, routed it, and captured the Spanish viceroy José de la Serna on the field.

The viceroy signed a capitulation that day surrendering all remaining Spanish forces in Peru — ending, with the stroke of a pen, three centuries of Spanish empire on the continent that had begun with the conquest of the Inca almost in these same mountains.
Mopping up remained — the fortress of Real Felipe at Callao held out under siege into 1826, the very last royalist stronghold to fall — but the continental war was effectively over at Ayacucho.

Upper Peru, the silver country claimed by both Peru and the Río de la Plata, chose with Sucre's encouragement to become an independent nation in 1825 and named itself Bolivia for the Liberator, with Sucre as its first president.

Bolívar wrote Bolivia a constitution that revealed how far his thinking had hardened: it provided for a president-for-life — a near-monarchy in republican dress — which his multiplying critics saw as exactly the kind of king they had fought to abolish.

In a little over fifteen years roughly twenty future nations came into being, an entire continental empire dissolved, and formal monarchy was swept off most of a hemisphere — yet the men who won it were already uneasy about the harder questions the war had not answered.

title: Mexico's Two-Stage Revolution
bullets: Mexico won its independence twice, aimed in opposite directions: a furious uprising of the poor in 1810 that the elites crushed, and a conservative break from Spain in 1821 led by those same elites to preserve the old order.

The first stage began with a church bell: in September 1810 the creole priest Miguel Hidalgo issued the Cry of Dolores, calling his largely Indigenous and mestizo parishioners to rise against bad government and the hated Spanish-born gachupines.

What answered was not an army but a flood of tens of thousands swelling toward 80,000, a vengeful explosion of rage against three centuries of casta that sometimes massacred Spaniards and creoles — so the wealthy creoles, seeing the nightmare of Haiti, mostly threw in with the royalists.

Despite his numbers Hidalgo commanded an untrained multitude, was shattered at Calderón Bridge in January 1811, then captured and executed, his severed head caged on a public building in Guanajuato for a decade as a warning.

The insurgency revived under a far abler priest, José María Morelos, who waged a disciplined guerrilla war, became a legend defending Cuautla, and convened a congress in 1813–14 that declared independence and called for an end to slavery and the caste system.

It was not enough: the creole elite's hostility and superior royalist organization closed in, and in 1815 Morelos was captured, tried by the Inquisition, defrocked, and shot, after which the first revolution survived only as scattered guerrillas under Vicente Guerrero.

What flipped Mexico came from Spain: the 1820 liberal revolt forced Ferdinand VII to restore the Constitution of 1812, and that anticlerical, reformist government horrified Mexico's conservatives, who now saw independence as the way to preserve their world.

The ruthless royalist officer Agustín de Iturbide turned that calculation into a country, opening secret talks with Guerrero and proclaiming the Plan of Iguala in 1821 — built on the Three Guarantees of independence, the Catholic Church, and equality between Spaniards and Americans.

The masterpiece of having-it-both-ways won independence in months with almost no fighting, but Iturbide then crowned himself Emperor Agustín I; the broke, divided First Mexican Empire collapsed within a year under the Plan of Casa Mata, and he was later shot.

Mexico became a republic under its first president Guadalupe Victoria, and the road it had traveled inverted everyone else's — the radicals lost and were martyred, the conservatives won their compromise nation with Church and hierarchy intact, the egalitarian promise deferred for generations.

title: Brazil's Bloodless Break
bullets: Everything about Brazil's independence is the opposite of Spanish America's: its king came to live there in person, the colony grew into a kingdom, and the break was declared by the heir to the throne himself, with almost no bloodshed and a single unified monarchy as the result.

When the Portuguese court fled to Rio in 1808, the king's arrival created a capital rather than a vacuum, and the prince regent John VI opened Brazil's ports to free trade and filled the colony with banks, presses, academies, and the apparatus of statehood.

In 1815 John elevated Brazil from colony to a co-equal kingdom joined with Portugal — promoted out of colonial status without a shot — dissolving most of the grievances that drove Spanish creoles to war and leaving far less to rebel against.

The arrangement could not last: after Napoleon's defeat a liberal revolution in Portugal in 1820 demanded the king return to Lisbon and Brazil be put back in its place, and in 1821 John sailed home — but first installed his son Pedro as regent with the advice to lead any break himself.

When Lisbon ordered Pedro home like a recalled child, he refused on the Dia do Fico in January 1822 — 'tell the people that I stay' — the first open defiance, an heir to the Portuguese throne siding with his Brazilian subjects.

The decisive moment came that September beside the stream Ipiranga, where Pedro proclaimed independence with 'Independence or death!' — the Cry of Ipiranga — and was crowned Emperor Pedro I of a new and enormous Brazilian Empire, with the statesman José Bonifácio as its organizing brain.

Brazil stayed one empire while Spanish America fragmented for converging reasons: a legitimate monarchy gave instant legitimacy and a single focus of loyalty, there was no shattering fifteen-year war, it had been one Portuguese domain, and a slave-heavy elite valued a strong center.

Keeping it one country took force: in 1824 the resentful northeast rose and proclaimed the breakaway Confederation of the Equator, which Pedro crushed hard, executing its leaders — centralization won in Brazil where it failed almost everywhere in Spanish America.

Pedro I was restless and quarrelsome, distracted by inheriting and then renouncing the Portuguese throne and by losing the Cisplatine War that turned the Banda Oriental into independent Uruguay in 1828; worn down, he abdicated the Brazilian throne in 1831.

After turbulent regency years his Brazilian-raised son was crowned Emperor Pedro II in 1840, and under his long, stable reign Brazil became genuinely exceptional — a durable constitutional monarchy in a continent of caudillos, delivering the stable center Spanish America so conspicuously lacked.

title: The Broken Dream and the Caudillos
bullets: The wars were won, and then the winners discovered the cruelest truth: defeating an empire is far easier than building a nation, and the same struggle that freed Spanish America had wrecked its economies, killed a generation, and left victorious generals with armies and no authority above them.

The biggest dream collapsed first: Gran Colombia was ungovernable from birth — its three regions separated by jungle and mountains, bolted together by war rather than common life — and split open over the founding argument of Latin American politics.

That argument set Bolívar, convinced only a strong centralized hand could save fragile nations from anarchy, against his vice-president Francisco de Paula Santander, the constitutionalist 'Man of Laws' who wanted civilian, federal government with power checked and spread.

Bolívar chose the strong hand, assuming dictatorial powers in 1828; an assassination attempt that year was foiled when Manuela Sáenz held off the attackers and helped him escape, earning her the title 'Liberator of the Liberator.'

Dictatorship could not hold together regions that no longer wished to be one country: in 1830 Venezuela broke away under the llanero hero José Antonio Páez and Ecuador under another general, and Gran Colombia dissolved into the three nations it had always been.

It was the end of everything for Bolívar — stripped of power, reviled, and struck by the assassination of his heir Sucre — and he died near Santa Marta in December 1830 at forty-seven, leaving the bitter verdict that those who served the revolution had 'plowed the sea.'

San Martín met a quieter version of the same fate, dying near Boulogne in France in 1850, largely forgotten — the two men who freed a continent both died abroad and embittered, only later dug up and rebuilt into marble national heroes.

Into the vacuum stepped the caudillo, the personalist strongman who seized power by force of arms and personality rather than institutions — the natural product of a world where the most powerful things were armies and the checks on them barely existed.

The most formidable ruled the south: in Argentina the cattle baron Juan Manuel de Rosas dominated for nearly two decades from 1835 through popular support, federalist ideology, the cult of his person, and the mazorca's secret-police terror, until he was overthrown by force in 1852.

Chile was the great exception that proved the pattern, where the conservative minister Diego Portales built a stable, impersonal state with his 1833 constitution — and Sarmiento's 1845 book Facundo gave the whole tragedy its voice as a war of 'civilization and barbarism.'

title: The Unfinished Century
bullets: The wars of independence ended around 1825, but the era of independence — working out what the new nations would actually be — ran on to 1903 and did not end gently, with savage wars, slavery dismantled half a century late, a monarchy falling, and a new hegemon rising to the north.

The most shocking fact of the period is how savagely the new nations fought each other, the worst being the War of the Triple Alliance (1864–1870), in which Paraguay under the dictator Francisco Solano López somehow ended up at war with Brazil, Argentina, and Uruguay at once.

Solano López waged a hopeless total war and refused every surrender until he was hunted down in 1870, by which point Paraguay was depopulated to a horrifying degree — the most-cited estimates put its losses well over half its people, though historians genuinely dispute the figures.

The War of the Pacific (1879–1883) pitted Chile against Peru and Bolivia over the nitrate- and guano-rich Atacama desert; stable, effective Chile won decisively, seizing the coast and leaving Bolivia the landlocked country it remains, still nursing the grievance.

The great unfinished business was slavery: most of Spanish America had abolished it grudgingly by mid-century, but Brazil, the hemisphere's largest slave society, clung to it longest, dismantling it only in agonizing stages.

Abolition came in stages — the 1850 end of the Atlantic slave trade, the 1871 Rio Branco 'Law of the Free Womb' — and finally on May 13, 1888, Princess Regent Isabel signed the Lei Áurea, abolishing slavery outright; Brazil was the last country in the Western Hemisphere to do so.

Abolition took a throne with it: when the Lei Áurea freed the slaves without compensation, the great slaveholding landowners withdrew their loyalty, and in 1889 a military coup under Deodoro da Fonseca deposed Pedro II and proclaimed the Brazilian Republic — extinguishing formal monarchy across the Americas.

Two bookends pointing to the future closed the century, both marking a new dominant power: in 1898 the United States, citing the renewed Cuban struggle launched by José Martí and the explosion of the USS Maine, crushed Spain in the Spanish–American War and stripped it of Cuba, Puerto Rico, and the Philippines.

In 1903 Panama broke from Colombia — not in a war against Europe but because the United States, wanting a canal Colombia had balked at, backed and protected the secession — the last nation of the independence century born from the ambitions of the rising power to the north, foreshadowed by the 1823 Monroe Doctrine.

Independence accomplished something world-historical — some twenty nations, monarchy swept off a hemisphere, the modern map drawn — but the deeper revolution was left unfinished: caste outlived the wars, slavery survived in Brazil to 1888, the united Spanish America shattered, and foreign domination began to be replaced by a new one.
